marrow__ANAT_CH26_Q001.takeaway: Pterygoid branch arises from petrous ICA, not cavernous ICA.
marrow__ANAT_CH26_Q001.displayText: The pterygoid branch is not a cavernous-part branch of the internal carotid artery; it arises from the petrous part. Angiography of the carotid siphon shows its multiple bends and characteristic S-shaped shadow. The source angiogram depicts the internal carotid artery segments.

rationales.a: Inferior hypophyseal artery is a cavernous-part branch; the pterygoid branch arises from petrous ICA.
rationales.b: Meningeal branches arise from the cavernous ICA, unlike pterygoid branch.
rationales.c: Cavernous branch arises from cavernous segment; pterygoid branch is petrous.

marrow__ANAT_CH26_Q003.takeaway: Posterior communicating artery arises from cerebral ICA and may form a compressive aneurysm causing CN III palsy.
marrow__ANAT_CH26_Q003.displayText: Ptosis, a down-and-out eye, and a dilated pupil suggest oculomotor palsy from a posterior communicating artery aneurysm. The posterior communicating artery is a branch of the cerebral part of the internal carotid artery. The source figure shows posterior communicating arteries in the circle of Willis.
emphasis: cerebral part of the internal carotid artery

rationales.a: Posterior cerebral artery is a basilar terminal branch, not the origin of posterior communicating artery.
rationales.b: Basilar artery supplies posterior circulation; the aneurysm-bearing posterior communicating artery arises from internal carotid.
rationales.d: Middle cerebral artery supplies lateral hemisphere and does not give rise to posterior communicating artery.

marrow__ANAT_CH26_Q004.takeaway: Basilar and anterior spinal arteries are unpaired.
marrow__ANAT_CH26_Q004.displayText: Basilar and anterior spinal arteries are unpaired CNS vessels. Basilar artery is a single vessel formed by union of the two vertebral arteries. Anterior spinal artery is formed by a branch from each vertebral artery near its termination. The source contrasts paired and unpaired arteries.
emphasis: Basilar and anterior spinal arteries are unpaired

rationales.a: Basilar artery is unpaired, formed by vertebral artery union; the question also includes another unpaired vessel.
rationales.b: Vertebral arteries are paired before joining to form basilar artery.
rationales.c: Anterior spinal artery is also unpaired, formed by joining branches of both vertebral arteries; thus both A and C are correct.

marrow__ANAT_CH26_Q005.takeaway: AICA is the most common origin of labyrinthine artery.
marrow__ANAT_CH26_Q005.displayText: The labyrinthine artery most commonly arises from the anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA), though it can occasionally arise directly from the basilar artery. The basilar artery is formed by union of the vertebral arteries and divides into the two posterior cerebral arteries at the upper border of the pons.
emphasis: though it can occasionally arise directly

rationales.a: Basilar artery can be a direct alternative origin, but it is not the most common source.
rationales.c: Superior cerebellar artery arises from basilar artery and is not the usual labyrinthine origin.
rationales.d: PICA is a vertebral branch; labyrinthine artery most commonly arises from AICA.

marrow__ANAT_CH26_Q006.takeaway: MCA is not a component of the circle of Willis.
marrow__ANAT_CH26_Q006.displayText: Blood in basal cisterns with xanthochromic CSF indicates subarachnoid hemorrhage. The circle of Willis does not include the middle cerebral artery. It lies in the interpeduncular fossa and forms an anastomosis between internal carotid and vertebrobasilar circulations. Components are anterior communicating artery, both anterior cerebral arteries, both internal carotid arteries, both posterior communicating arteries, both posterior cerebral arteries, and basilar artery.
emphasis: circle of Willis does not include the middle cerebral artery

rationales.a: Anterior cerebral arteries are part of the circle of Willis.
rationales.c: Posterior communicating arteries connect ICA and PCA and are included in the circle.
rationales.d: Posterior cerebral arteries are components; MCA branches laterally from ICA but is not part of the arterial ring.

marrow__ANAT_CH26_Q007.takeaway: MCA supplies lateral motor cortex except the leg area, typically spared in MCA stroke.
marrow__ANAT_CH26_Q007.displayText: Middle cerebral artery supplies most of the lateral cerebral hemisphere, including nearly all motor cortex except the leg area; an MCA lesion can cause contralateral hemiparesis sparing the leg. Anterior cerebral artery is the smaller terminal internal-carotid branch, runs in the sagittal fissure, supplies medial cortex and some lentiform, caudate and internal-capsule regions, and anastomoses with posterior cerebral artery. MCA is the larger terminal branch, travels in lateral sulcus and supplies most lateral hemisphere except a narrow superior strip and occipital/inferolateral temporal regions. Posterior cerebral artery is the basilar terminal branch supplying occipital lobe, inferolateral and medial temporal surfaces, and parts of brainstem.
emphasis: MCA lesion can cause contralateral hemiparesis sparing the leg

rationales.a: PCA supplies occipital cortex and is not the main lateral motor supply.
rationales.b: ACA supplies medial frontal/parietal cortex, including leg area, spared in the described MCA pattern.
rationales.d: ACA plus MCA would include the leg-sparing cortical territory; the vessel causing the described distribution is MCA.

marrow__ANAT_CH26_Q008.takeaway: PCA occipital infarction may spare macular vision and cause Riddoch phenomenon.
marrow__ANAT_CH26_Q008.displayText: Occipital-lobe ischemia from posterior cerebral artery occlusion can cause homonymous field loss, hallucinations, Anton syndrome and Riddoch phenomenon (perception of moving targets despite blindness to stationary targets). Macular vision is often spared: peripheral-field visual cortex is supplied by PCA, while the calcarine tip representing central macular vision may receive middle cerebral artery branches.

rationales.a: MCA supplies lateral cortex; occipital visual cortex and macular-sparing pattern localize to PCA territory.
rationales.c: PICA supplies lateral medulla and cerebellum, not occipital visual cortex.
rationales.d: Posterior choroidal artery is a PCA branch, not the main cortical artery causing this field defect.

marrow__ANAT_CH26_Q009.displayText: The middle cerebral artery is the chief artery of the superolateral cerebral hemisphere. Anterior cerebral artery supplies only a narrow superior strip of that surface; most of it is supplied by MCA. Anterior cerebral artery is the chief supply of the medial brain surface, and posterior cerebral artery is chief for the inferior surface. “Lateral cerebral artery” is not an artery.

rationales.c: PCA chiefly supplies occipital and inferomedial temporal territories.
rationales.d: “Lateral cerebral artery” is not an artery; the real named artery supplying most superolateral cortex is MCA.

marrow__ANAT_CH26_Q010.takeaway: PCA supplies occipital/temporal territories and deep central structures, not the pons.
marrow__ANAT_CH26_Q010.displayText: The marked vessel is the posterior cerebral artery; it does not supply the pons. PCA cortical branches supply visual cortex in occipital lobe and medial/inferolateral temporal surfaces. Central branches supply thalamus, subthalamus, lentiform nucleus, midbrain, pineal gland, superior and inferior colliculi, and medial/lateral geniculate bodies. Choroidal branches supply choroid plexus of lateral and third ventricles.

rationales.a: PCA supplies choroid plexus of the third ventricle through choroidal branches.
rationales.b: PCA supplies midbrain and colliculi through central branches.
rationales.d: PCA central branches supply lentiform nucleus; the pons is the listed structure outside its territory.

marrow__ANAT_CH26_Q011.takeaway: PICA is the largest vertebral branch and supplies lateral medulla/cerebellum.
marrow__ANAT_CH26_Q011.displayText: The syndrome is Wallenberg (lateral medullary) syndrome and the marked vessel is vertebral artery. Its largest branch is PICA. Vertebral artery arises from first part of subclavian, enters skull through foramen magnum and joins the opposite vertebral artery to form basilar artery. Cranial branches include meningeal branches to posterior fossa dura, posterior spinal arteries to posterior cord third, anterior spinal artery to anterior cord two-thirds, PICA to lateral medulla/cerebellar hemisphere/fourth-ventricle choroid plexus, and medullary branches.

rationales.a: Anterior spinal artery supplies anterior spinal cord, not the largest branch producing lateral medullary syndrome.
rationales.b: Posterior spinal artery supplies posterior spinal cord territory.
rationales.d: Medullary branches supply medulla, but PICA is the largest vertebral branch and matches Wallenberg syndrome.

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of a Charcot-Bouchard aneurysm. The affected artery is
the Charcot's artery which is the striate branch of the middle cerebral artery marked as 'C' in the
above image.

are commonly associated with hypertension. Charcot's artery supplies the internal capsule and
basal ganglia. It is also known as the 'Charcot's artery of cerebral haemorrhage'.
